Subject: SLO qualification: token bounds & latency impact — next steps

Hi Aminah — great to meet today, thanks for the detailed product walk-through. Quick recap and proposed next steps so nothing falls through the cracks.

Call recap (short):
- Business goal: embed long-form summarization and Q&A into MedIntel’s reports UI. Want progressive token streaming while authoring and a final long-form generation for export.
- Target SLO: p95 generation latency target discussed at ~120–200 ms for typical responses; you called out a stretch of 200 ms p95 for interactive UX but said some back-end exports could tolerate higher.
- Concurrency / throughput: target sustained concurrency ~150–200 requests/sec at peak; typical baseline ~40 rps.
- Typical payloads: most queries are short (100–400 input tokens) but export jobs can be large. You mentioned output up to ~4k tokens and occasional large uploads for context (~6–10k tokens).
- Streaming: required for the editor (partial tokens as they arrive). Exports can be non-streaming.

Primary open questions for qualification:
1) Can you share representative sample payloads (input + expected output sizes) and 2–3 peak-minute concurrency windows?
2) Confirm whether context is entirely user-provided or if server-side retrieval (DB + embeddings) expands context at generation time.
3) Any hard latency SLOs for exports vs interactive flows?

Proposed next steps (we can run these quickly):
- MedIntel provides sample payloads and 1-hour peak waveform (we can accept anonymized data).
- We schedule a 2-hour SLO simulation on Dedicated or Hosted staging depending on data policies. SLO sim will exercise: peak concurrency, large context scenarios, and streaming delivery.
- We’ll share an SLO simulation plan + quick config recommendations (quantization, batching, prefix caching) — attached draft.

Attachments: slo-sim-plan.pdf (sim plan + metrics we’ll collect), sample-payloads.json (placeholder format).

If that all sounds right, can you confirm by EOD and point to the engineering contact we should whitelist for the staging run? Also confirm whether you prefer Hosted with VPC peering (fastest to trial) or Redwood Dedicated (predictable throughput).

Cheers,

Jasmine Liu

Thanks Jasmine — good summary. A few clarifications from our side:

- Output sizes: 90% of interactive responses are under ~1k tokens. The 4k+ cases are for scheduled report exports (weekly/monthly).
- Context: user-provided plus server-augmented retrieval. Retrieval can add another 3–5k tokens in some cases (search results + metadata). So total context occasionally hits ~10–11k tokens.
- Streaming: critical for editor UX — we need partial tokens within ~150–250 ms ideally for perceptual responsiveness. Final export latency can be higher (up to several seconds).
- SLO preference: for interactive flows we’d like p95 <= 200 ms, p99 < 500 ms if achievable. Exports: p95 <= 5 s OK.

We’ll attach a redacted sample-payloads.json with three representative cases. I’ll also loop in our lead infra person (ops@medintel.com) for whitelist + network details.

Going to confirm preferred trial mode — leaning Dedicated trial for capacity guarantees.

Best,

Hi Aminah — thanks for the quick clarifications. I want to call out a few technical trade-offs and a concrete plan so expectations are aligned before we run the sim.

Technical notes (short):
- Context window effect: end-to-end generation latency is a function of both request size (input tokens) and model attended context. For decoder-style models, attention over larger contexts increases memory pressure and can add non-linear token-generation latency at longer sequence lengths. Empirically, going from a 4k to 10k context can add ~25–60% generation latency depending on model variant and hardware.
- Streaming latency tradeoffs: streaming reduces perceived latency for users but doesn’t reduce total cost. For high concurrency, streaming still requires the same underlying throughput; it shifts payloads from a single bulk response to many small flushes which can increase request overhead unless we batch efficiently on the runtime.
- Batching vs latency: continuous batching improves throughput but increases per-request latency depending on batch windows. At strict p95 targets (~150–200 ms) we recommend conservative batching (small batch size, low wait time) or single-request fast-paths on dedicated nodes.
- Quantization and kernel choices: 8-bit quantization will typically reduce latency and memory, but some long-context kernels have better numeric stability in 16-bit. We’ll pick model variants tuned for long context if context regularly exceeds 8k tokens.

Recommendation & plan:
1) For the sim we suggest two runs: Hosted-staging (VPC peered) with model variant A (quantized) to validate streaming behavior and Dedicated trial with model variant B (long-context optimized) to show throughput at 150–200 rps.
2) Collect metrics: per-token latency distribution, p50/p95/p99, KV cache hit rate, GPU utilization, batching windows, and TCP-level traces. We’ll correlate response tail latency with context length.
3) Target outcomes: show a configuration that meets interactive p95 <= 200 ms for 90% of your typical interactive traces and demonstrate export throughput for 4k–8k outputs under controlled load. If we need lower tails (p99 < 500 ms) we’ll recommend further capacity or edge routing.

Practical asks from you before we run the sim:
- Confirm the engineering point of contact for IP whitelisting and whether we can test with anonymized but realistic payloads.
- Approve a 2-hour Dedicated trial window and confirm timezone for scheduling (we’ll propose 48 hours notice).

I attached a short network-trace template and the SLO sim plan.
